summary: Provides a guideline for creating country-specific civic address considerations documents, as required by RFC 4776. It also creates an IANA registry for such documents and registers the one for Austria. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Addresses are written differently in different countries. This document sets up a list where each country can explain its rules, and begins with Austria.

subtitle: How to write a country's rules for mapping civic addresses into PIDF-LO, plus the IANA registry that lists them.

tldr.problem: Real-world address data differs from country to country and does not match PIDF-LO's civic address elements, so different implementers can map the same data differently, which hurts interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives requirements and a workflow for writing a civic address considerations document per data source, element-by-element guidelines, and an IANA registry (Expert Review) that points to such documents; Austria is registered as the first example.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 4776 and replaces its instructions for writing considerations documents. The examples in RFC 4776 for Canada, Germany, Japan, Korea and the United States are registered as obsolete.

today: RFC 5774 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 154) that updates RFC 4776. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Mapping Problem
sections.content:
The Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO, RFC 4119) carries geographical information on the Internet, including civic addresses built from a set of civic address types (CAtypes). In many uses it is filled in from long-established sources such as postal and governmental building registers or official residents registers. Their structure and format almost always differ from the CAtype definitions, and they differ from country to country.

Without guidelines for mapping source Fields into CAtype Elements, different creators of PIDF-LO documents may get different results from the same data source. That reduces interoperability and raises the risk of misinterpretation. RFC 4776 asked for country-specific considerations documents but defined neither their structure nor a way to publish them. This RFC supplies both.

The guidelines focus on formal use, such as conveying location during an emergency call, and are not meant to forbid informal uses such as PIDF-LO exchanged in an instant-messaging session.
sections.plainLanguage: If two people fill in the same address form using different habits, the computer cannot tell it is the same place. Writing down the habit for each country fixes that.

sections.title: Requirements for a Considerations Document
sections.content:
A document that defines civic-address mapping considerations has to meet these requirements:

  • It MUST identify the data source and SHOULD briefly describe its structure.
  • Only one active mapping definition should exist per data source, to reduce ambiguity.
  • It MUST give instructions for every Field in the data, saying whether the Field is required, optional or must not be used.
  • It MUST give instructions for every CAtype Element registered when the document is created, with the same three levels of use. If the IETF revises the CAtypes, the document SHOULD be updated, and the existing mapping stays in force until then.
  • Mapping procedures SHOULD be reversible, so recipients can find the original record.
  • Every required or optional Field MUST have at least one example mapping.
  • Access restrictions on the source data MUST also be imposed on the resulting PIDF-LO documents.

The RFC points out that even if the national mapping is unclear to an outsider, the country Element tells which context created the PIDF-LO. A consistent mapping also matters for checking whether two PIDF-LO documents describe the same location.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipe card for a country has to list every ingredient on the form, say which are needed, and show an example, so anyone can follow it the same way.

sections.title: The Workflow for Writing One
sections.content:
The workflow has five steps: describe the data source; identify every Field and decide whether it is used for PIDF-LO; give a clear mapping instruction for each used Field; list all registered CAtypes and their level of use; and provide examples of source data and mapping results.

Where a Field has the same meaning as a CAtype, it SHOULD map directly to that Element. If a Field does not fit any CAtype, new Elements are not an option unless the IETF specifies new generic CAtypes. The choices are then to concatenate several Fields into one Element (defining delimiters so the parts can be retrieved again) or to use an Element that is otherwise unused. Concatenation is required when there are more Fields than Elements. The xml:lang attribute should be present in PIDF-LO XML documents, according to RFC 5139.
sections.plainLanguage: Go through the form box by box. If a box has no matching slot, either squeeze two things into one slot with a clear divider, or use a slot nobody else is using.

sections.title: Guidelines for Individual Elements
sections.content:
Section 4.2 goes element by element, and recommends that considerations documents follow a similar structure.

  • Country: holds the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code in uppercase. It cannot be redefined nationally, since it identifies which national mapping was used.
  • A1 to A6: national subdivisions, with A1 the top level. A document MUST state whether A1 uses ISO 3166-2 codes exclusively or a defined list of values, and A1 MUST NOT be redefined for another use.
  • Road and street names: the document says which of RD, RDSEC, RDBR, RDSUBADDR, PRM, POM, PRD, POD and STS are used. Use of A6 for street names is no longer valid.
  • House numbers: if the structure fits HNO and HNS, the document MUST mandate those; otherwise it MUST define a mapping strategy, with abbreviations and delimiters clearly defined.
  • Local names: LMK, LOC and NAM; where several values occur, concatenation with ; is recommended unless that character appears in the source.
  • Floors: FLR; the document SHOULD say whether numbers, text or both are allowed.
  • Address codes: ADDCODE MAY carry a code that identifies the record. Where it is used, its relation to the other Elements MUST be stated.
  • Other elements: UNIT, ROOM and SEAT for places inside a building, PC, PCN and POBOX for postal codes, and PLC and BLD for place type and building.
sections.plainLanguage: Each slot on the address form gets its own short rule: which country code to use, how to write the floor, what to do with a farm's name. That way nobody has to guess.

sections.title: The IANA Registry
sections.content:
IANA created the PIDF-LO Civic Address Considerations Registry. Each entry has a Country-Code (an ISO 3166 alpha-2 code, or other), a Serial Number assigned by IANA per Country-Code starting at zero and never reused, a reference to the document, a requestor and a status of active or obsolete. The Country-Code and Serial Number together identify an entry, for example AT-0 or US-1.

New entries are added after Expert Review under RFC 5226. The Expert checks conformance with the guidelines in this RFC and, if in doubt, SHOULD consult the GEOPRIV mailing list or its dedicated successor. Requesters SHOULD use the template in the RFC, and the template SHOULD be contained in the considerations document itself.

The RFC registers the Austrian considerations from its Appendix A, and also registers the RFC 4776 considerations for Canada, Germany, Japan, Korea and the United States as obsolete (entries CA-0, DE-0, JP-0, KR-0 and US-0).
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps a library shelf. Each country can put its address rule book on it, and a helper checks the book before it goes on the shelf. Old books get a stamp saying they are out of date.

sections.title: The Austrian Example
sections.content:
Appendix A is a complete considerations document for the Austrian Building and Habitation Registry, operated by Statistik Austria GmbH. The registry describes estates, buildings and usable units. The data format is publicly available, while data access is restricted.

The body of the RFC uses Austria for its examples. The country Element is AT, A1 to A5 hold province, district, commune, village and cadastral municipality, and A6 must not be used. RD holds the street name, and the other road Elements must not be used. Austrian house numbers are concatenated into HNO with delimiters, and HNS is not allowed. NAM carries the local name (Vulgoname), LMK the farm name, and FLR uses numbers or text, with the street-level floor written EG or 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Austria goes first as a worked example, showing exactly which part of an Austrian address goes into which slot, even for farm names and half floors.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The security section is a single sentence: RFC 4119 contains general security considerations for handling PIDF-LOs. The one related rule in the body is that access restrictions on a source data set MUST also be imposed on the PIDF-LO documents made from it, and a considerations document SHOULD note such restrictions in its own Security Considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: If the original address list is private, the forms made from it must stay private too.
